facts.statehood_note: Florida entered the Union as a state where slavery was legal. Spain handed Florida to the United States under the Adams-Onís Treaty (signed 1819, in effect 1821), and Florida was a U.S. territory from 1822 to 1845.
facts.motto: In God We Trust (on the state seal since 1868; made the official motto in 2006)
borders: Gulf of Mexico (called the Gulf of America by U.S. agencies such as NOAA)

symbols.name: Florida panther (1982, chosen by a vote of students across the state; the most endangered of Florida's symbols)

facts.name_origin: In 1513 Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León called the land La Pascua Florida, for its green, flowering landscape and because it was the Easter season, which Spaniards called Pascua Florida (Festival of Flowers).

government.chambers: Florida Senate (40 senators, 4-year terms) and Florida House of Representatives (120 representatives)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; a governor who has served more than six years in two terms in a row cannot be elected to the next term). The constitution says the governor holds "the supreme executive power" and must "take care that the laws be faithfully executed." Florida also elects a Cabinet: the attorney general, chief financial officer and commissioner of agriculture.
government.courts: Florida Supreme Court (7 justices). The state's judicial power belongs to the Supreme Court, the district courts of appeal, circuit courts and county courts.
government.local: 67 counties (Palm Beach is the largest by area and Union the smallest; Miami-Dade has the most people). The Seminole Tribe of Florida and the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida have their own tribal governments.
government.constitution: Florida's current constitution was revised in 1968 and has been amended since. Earlier constitutions came in 1838 (written before statehood), 1861, 1865, 1868 and 1885.
government.kid_line: "The seat of government shall be the City of Tallahassee, in Leon County." (Florida Constitution, Article II, Section 2)

long_ago.about: The Calusa built a powerful fishing chiefdom on the southwest coast, from Charlotte Harbor to Marco Island. They lived from the estuaries instead of farming, and their capital town of Calos was probably at Mound Key, which they built up with shells.

About 35 Timucua chiefdoms lived in northeast and north-central Florida and southeast Georgia. They farmed corn, beans and squash, fished and hunted, and lived where Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565.

The Apalachee lived in the panhandle between the Aucilla and Ochlockonee rivers, near present-day Tallahassee. They grew corn, beans and squash, and some of their mounds are protected at Lake Jackson Mounds Archaeological State Park.

The Tequesta lived on Biscayne Bay, where Miami is today, by fishing and gathering. The Miami Circle, a ring of holes about 38 feet across cut into the bedrock at a Tequesta village site, is a clue to their life.

today.about: Federally recognized since 1957, with reservations at Hollywood, Big Cypress, Brighton, Immokalee, Fort Pierce and Tampa; it runs the Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum on the Big Cypress Reservation.

today.nation: Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida
today.about: Federally recognized since 1962, with lands along the Tamiami Trail in the Everglades; Buffalo Tiger was its first elected chairman.

first_peoples.today_note: Florida's original nations shrank sharply under Spanish rule, mostly from new diseases, and from the late 1600s raiders from the north, sometimes joined by Carolina colonists, burned villages and carried captives away to be sold into slavery. Spain took the few survivors to Cuba in 1763. Creek and other Indigenous people then moved into Florida and formed the Seminole and Miccosukee nations. The U.S. forced more than 3,000 Seminole people west of the Mississippi in the 1800s, and today's Florida Seminole and Miccosukee descend from the few hundred who stayed and never surrendered.
sites: Mound Key, probably the site of the Calusa capital town of Calos
Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum, Big Cypress Reservation (run by the Seminole Tribe of Florida)
Lake Jackson Mounds Archaeological State Park, Tallahassee (Apalachee and earlier mound builders)

history.event: The first people reach the Florida peninsula, following big game like mastodons and mammoths across grasslands.
The Mississippian culture, with farming towns and earthen mounds, reaches into Florida.
Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León reaches Florida and names it La Pascua Florida.
The Calusa drive off Ponce de León's attempt to start a colony near Charlotte Harbor; he is wounded and later dies in Cuba.
Spain founds St. Augustine on Timucua land, the first permanent European settlement in what is now the United States.
Workers build the stone Castillo de San Marcos in St. Augustine.

Spanish governor Manuel de Montiano founds Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose (Fort Mose), the first legally sanctioned free Black town in what is now the United States, for Africans who escaped slavery in the English colonies. In 1740 British troops from Georgia capture Fort Mose, and in June the Fort Mose militia, led by Francisco Menéndez, retakes it in a surprise attack later called Bloody Mose.
The First Seminole War: Andrew Jackson invades Spanish Florida and pushes the Seminole farther south.
Spain hands Florida to the United States under the Adams-Onís Treaty, and Florida becomes a U.S. territory.
After the Indian Removal Act of 1830, the United States tries to force the Seminole west, starting the Second Seminole War. Seminole leader Osceola is seized under a flag of truce in 1837.
On March 3, Florida becomes the 27th state, a state where slavery is legal. By 1860, 61,745 of Florida's 140,424 people (about 44%) are enslaved.
On January 10, Florida secedes from the Union and joins the Confederacy. About 1,044 Black Floridians later serve in the Union Army.
On May 20, Union General Edward McCook reads the Emancipation Proclamation in Tallahassee, officially ending slavery in Florida. May 20 is Florida's Emancipation Day.
During Reconstruction, Jonathan C. Gibbs becomes Florida's secretary of state (1868) and Josiah T. Walls becomes Florida's first Black member of Congress (1871).

trailblazers.name: Francisco Menéndez
trailblazers.group: African-born freedom seeker and militia captain
trailblazers.text: A Mandinga man born in West Africa, he escaped slavery in Carolina, fought alongside the Yamasee, and reached Spanish Florida, where he was enslaved again. In 1726 the Spanish governor made him commander of St. Augustine's Black militia, and after years of petitions Governor Manuel de Montiano granted him and other freedom seekers unconditional freedom in 1738. He led Fort Mose, a town of about 100 free Black people, and in June 1740 led the surprise attack that retook it from British troops; when Spain gave Florida to Britain in 1763, the Fort Mose families moved to Cuba.

trailblazers.name: Mary McLeod Bethune
trailblazers.text: In 1904 she started a school for Black girls in Daytona with six students, and it grew into Bethune-Cookman University. She helped Black women register to vote. In 2022 her statue was unveiled in the U.S. Capitol, replacing a statue of a Confederate general.

trailblazers.name: Zora Neale Hurston
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, author and folklorist
trailblazers.text: She grew up in Eatonville, which in 1887 became one of the first all-Black towns incorporated in the United States, and later used it as the setting for many stories. She studied anthropology and collected folklore, and she wrote Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937).

trailblazers.name: Josiah T. Walls
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Virginia, he was captured by the Union Army in 1862, joined the U.S. Colored Troops in 1863, and settled in Alachua County after his discharge in Florida. In 1871 he became the first Black person elected to Congress from Florida, serving until 1876.

trailblazers.name: Marjory Stoneman Douglas
trailblazers.text: A Miami journalist, she wrote The Everglades: River of Grass (1947), which helped people see the Everglades as a living river instead of a worthless swamp. She spoke up for it for the rest of her life and lived to be 108.

trailblazers.name: Betty Mae Tiger Jumper
trailblazers.text: Born near Indiantown, she became the first Florida Seminole to finish high school and trained as a nurse. In 1967 she became the first woman elected to lead the Seminole Tribe of Florida, and she helped start the Seminole News.

trailblazers.name: Buffalo Tiger
trailblazers.text: He helped the Miccosukee win federal recognition in 1962 and served as the tribe's first elected chairman from 1962 to 1985. He worked so the Miccosukee could govern themselves and protect the Everglades.

waters: Lake Okeechobee (700 square miles, the largest lake)
St. Johns River (273 miles, the longest river)
geography.regions: Florida has the panhandle in the northwest, the peninsula with its lakes, springs and central ridges, the wide Everglades wetland in the south, and the chain of the Florida Keys, with about 1,350 miles of coastline.

ecosystems.name: The Everglades
ecosystems.about: The Everglades formed about 5,000 years ago on porous limestone. Everglades National Park, set aside in 1947 as the first national park created for its living things, protects 1.5 million acres where alligators, wading birds, turtles and fish live.

ecosystems.name: Mangrove forests
ecosystems.about: Salt-tolerant mangrove trees grow where Everglades fresh water mixes with salt water. They are a nursery for young sea animals, and they are the first line of defense against hurricane winds and storm surge.

ecosystems.name: Florida's Coral Reef
ecosystems.about: Florida's Coral Reef stretches more than 350 nautical miles from the Dry Tortugas to the St. Lucie Inlet in Martin County.

ecosystems.name: Springs
ecosystems.about: Florida's springs flow up from the aquifer underground, and the state has 33 first-magnitude springs. Manatees, Florida's state marine mammal, live in many of the state's waterways; they were moved from endangered to threatened in 2017.

science.weather: Florida is warm, with a wet season from about May to November. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 to November 30, and hurricanes can bring strong winds, flooding rain and storm surge; mangroves help shield the coast.
science.resources: Tourism, hospitality, agriculture (citrus, strawberries, sugarcane and cattle), real estate and transportation are big parts of Florida's economy, along with aerospace. Florida also has the country's largest deposits of rock phosphate, mostly in Bone Valley.
science.highlight: The Space Coast! Apollo 11 launched from Kennedy Space Center's Pad 39A on July 16, 1969, and made the first Moon landing on July 20.

g3_ss.title: Florida's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Tallahassee, learn what the governor and Legislature do, explore counties using DeSoto County as the example, read a real line from Florida's constitution, and meet Floridians who led and served.

g3_ss.title: Florida's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Calusa and Timucua of long ago and the Seminole Tribe and Miccosukee Tribe today, look at shell mounds and canoes as clues, and find Florida places with Indigenous names.

g3_ss.title: Florida Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Discover Fort Mose and Francisco Menéndez, Zora Neale Hurston of Eatonville, Mary McLeod Bethune and Betty Mae Tiger Jumper, and be a Source Detective with a 1759 count of Fort Mose.

g45_ss.title: Florida's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Locate the Calusa, Timucua, Apalachee and Tequesta, compare fishing and farming nations, investigate shell mounds, artifacts and Spanish records, and tell honestly what happened after Europeans arrived.

g45_ss.title: Spanish Florida and Fort Mose
g45_ss.plan: Trace St. Augustine and the Castillo de San Marcos, Spain's 1693 offer of freedom, Fort Mose under Captain Francisco Menéndez, and who benefited and who paid the cost in 1763.

g45_ss.title: Florida 1821–1877
g45_ss.plan: Study the Seminole Wars and Black Seminole allies, statehood as a state where slavery was legal, the Civil War and Florida's Emancipation Day (May 20, 1865), and Reconstruction leaders Jonathan C. Gibbs and Josiah T. Walls.

g3_sci.title: The Everglades: A River of Grass
g3_sci.plan: Learn why the Everglades is called a river of grass, meet alligators, spoonbills, panthers and manatees, find what living things need there, and meet Marjory Stoneman Douglas and others who protect it.

g3_sci.title: Hurricanes: How They Form and How Families Get Ready
g3_sci.plan: Learn what a hurricane needs to grow, find the calm eye, read a water temperature chart, pack a hurricane kit and meet the hurricane hunters.

g3_sci.title: Florida's Springs and Manatees
g3_sci.plan: Follow a raindrop into the aquifer, learn how springs bubble up clear water and why manatees swim to springs in winter, and read a manatee count chart.

g45_sci.title: Florida Ecosystems: River of Grass, Mangroves and Reefs
g45_sci.plan: Trace Everglades sheet flow from Lake Okeechobee to Florida Bay, build an Everglades food web, explain how mangroves and coral reefs protect the coast, and read wading bird nesting data.

g45_sci.title: Hurricanes and Florida Weather
g45_sci.plan: Explain how warm water and low pressure build a hurricane, use the Saffir-Simpson scale, explain storm surge, read a storm track table and meet National Hurricane Center scientists.

g45_sci.title: Florida's Space Coast
g45_sci.plan: Use latitude to explain why rockets launch from Florida's east coast, explain thrust and orbit, and trace the coast's story from the Ais people to Apollo, the shuttle and Artemis.
